description: SolarShield-AI is an AI-driven framework by Team MU Solar Pulse that analyzes solar activity, forecasts space weather risks, assesses potential impacts on Earth’s critical technologies, and generates explainable early warnings and preparedness recommendations.
summary: The SolarShield-AI is a space weather monitoring system that can provide early warnings of CubeSat drag caused by increased space weather activity. The system uses a combination of real-time and historical F10.7 solar flux, Kp geomagnetic activity, Dst, solar wind observations, and statistical trends in order to determine when space weather is likely to increase. Before generating alerts, the system performs several tests on the data to see if there is a significant change in space weather activity. These tests include Mann-Kendall significance tests, Sen's Slopes, rate-of-change calculations, and confidence interval analyses. All of the indicators are converted into either Low, Moderate, High, or Extreme risk categories for CubeSat drag based on their orbit altitude (300-400km, 400-500km, and 500-600km). A user interface allows users to view the primary factors contributing to the risk category, how confident the system is in its assessment, how current the data used was, and what operators should do in response to the alert. In addition to providing current information about space weather activity, the user interface allows users to replay previous events such as the October 2022 Starlink Storm. The primary purpose of the SolarShield-AI is to convert complex space weather data into a format that is understandable, useful, and provides users with a sense of uncertainty regarding the potential impact of space weather on satellites.
details:
SolarShield-AI is a user-friendly Streamlit dashboard that will assist users in identifying trend-based space weather conditions and providing early warning of potential CubeSat orbital-drag increases. The system will collect, normalize and preserve source data (F10.7 Solar Radio Flux, Kp Index, Dst Index, Solar Wind Speed, Solar Wind Density, IMF Bz) along with relevant metadata including: date/time of collection, data quality and historical data retrieval for reproducible analyses.

Figure 1: WebApp User Interface .

The trend detection software is designed to produce moving averages, rate-of-change measurements, and period-of-sustained-activity measurements. To evaluate whether the observed changes are significant enough to be considered valid, it uses the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s Slope method. If there is insufficient data available, or if the data used is no longer current, or if the data used does not meet statistical significance criteria, or if the level of uncertainty in the data makes it difficult to draw conclusions about trends, then the system will suppress alerts. If the system determines that the data provided has met all of these validation criteria, then the system will estimate drag risk across three different orbital altitude ranges – 300-400 km, 400-500 km, and 500-600 km.

Figure 2: Cycle-by-Cycle Mann-Kendall Trend Test Results and Sen’s Slope Estimates for Monthly Sunspot Numbers.

Each alert will include a risk level, probability estimate, confidence interval, validity period, data freshness, model version, and driver explanation. As an example, an alert can identify high Kp, elevated F10.7, and negative Dst as contributing factors to a potential event. In addition to providing information about the potential event, each alert will also recommend action items for you to take; these could include increasing your monitoring of the spacecraft, delaying the launch of the spacecraft, reviewing your orbit maintenance margins, or planning for an orbit correction.

Figure 3: Baseline Persistence Model Forecast Performance for Monthly Sunspot Numbers ($N = 129$, $\text{MAE} = 19.8$, $\text{RMSE} = 27.3$).

The user has the ability to view a re-creation of past events, such as the October 2022 Starlink geomagnetic storm, by viewing a "historical event replay" feature in the software. This will allow the user to see how well their simulated risk level compared to actual observed indicator values, and to gain insight into what type of impacts space weather may have on satellites in LEO (low Earth orbit).

Figure 4: Exploratory Analog Curve and Empirical 10–90% Uncertainty Band for Solar Cycle 26 ,27 onword.


The dashboard is built on top of several different technologies including Python, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Altair and various statistical analysis libraries. There are multiple software components that make up the system including; data ingestion, feature engineering, risk assessment, visualization, testing, and periodic data refresh processes. This project is unique in that it allows for the connection of space weather trends to support CubeSat mission planning based upon altitude-specific conditions as well as provide the ability to communicate complicated scientific information to both technical operator and student audiences.

The SolarShield-AI was developed with the consideration of; data quality, uncertainty, source traceability, temporal alignment, missing observations, model limitations, altitude sensitivity, spacecraft characteristics and responsible communication. The purpose of SolarShield-AI is to provide information for research, education and operational decision making, and also clearly delineate validated evidence from uncertainty. The long-term goal of SolarShield-AI is to assist satellite teams with preparations for changes in space weather, and to educate the general public on how solar activity impacts technology in space.
